qs.q: A 68-year-old man presents from a nursing home with fever, increased urinary frequency and urgency, and mental status changes. He has a penicillin allergy of anaphylaxis. Which of the following β-lactams is the most appropriate choice for gram-negative coverage of this patient's urinary tract infection?
qs.e: Aztreonam is a monobactam with no cross-reactivity with penicillins and can be safely given to penicillin-allergic patients, even those with anaphylaxis. Although cross-reactivity between cephalosporins/carbapenems and penicillins is low (<1-10%), the risk rarely outweighs the benefit in cases of documented anaphylaxis. Aztreonam provides good gram-negative coverage for UTI.

qs.q: Each of the following organisms is an important cause of urinary tract infections except
qs.e: *Bacteroides fragilis* is an anaerobe associated with intra-abdominal infections/abscesses, not a typical UTI pathogen; the other three are classic uropathogens.

qs.q: A 25-year-old sexually active female presents with urinary tract infection. The organism that is coagulase-negative and novobiocin resistant is
qs.e: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and causes UTI in young sexually active women, being the second most common cause of UTI after E. coli. S. epidermidis is novobiocin sensitive, which helps differentiate these two coagulase-negative staphylococci.

qs.q: A 23-year-old woman has a history of recurrent urinary tract infections, including at least one episode of pyelonephritis. Blood typing shows the P blood group antigen. Which of the following is likely to be the primary cause of her infections?
o: Escherichia coli that produce heat-stable toxin
Escherichia coli with K1 (capsular type 1) antigen
qs.e: P pili (P fimbriae) on uropathogenic E. coli specifically bind to P blood group antigens on uroepithelial cells. Patients with P antigens are more susceptible to pyelonephritis. P-piliated E. coli strains cause 90% of pyelonephritis cases in otherwise healthy individuals.

qs.q: The organism that is coagulase-negative and novobiocin-resistant is commonly Staphylococcus saprophyticus, which is a frequent cause of urinary tract infections in young, sexually active women.
qs.e: Staphylococcus saprophyticus is a common cause of urinary tract infections (UTIs) in women. It is characterized by being coagulase-negative and resistant to novobiocin. Staphylococcus epidermidis is also coagulase-negative but is typically sensitive to novobiocin.

rx.name: Urinary tract infection
first: Cystitis: nitrofurantoin for 3–5 days, or cotrimoxazole if susceptible

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Urinary tract infection (UTI) is an inflammation of the urinary system caused by bacteria, most often E. coli. Diagnosis relies on symptoms, urine dipstick, and culture. Management balances effective antibiotics with local resistance patterns and patient safety.

sections.p: UTI is an infection of any part of the urinary tract. Diagnosis starts with clinical suspicion, confirmed by a positive urine dipstick for leukocyte esterase or nitrites and a urine culture showing ≥10⁵ CFU/mL of a single organism.
b: Symptoms: dysuria, frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, fever.
Risk factors: female sex, catheter use, pregnancy, diabetes, structural abnormalities.

sections.p: UTI severity is staged by anatomic location and systemic involvement. Simple cystitis is uncomplicated; pyelonephritis is upper tract infection; urosepsis is systemic spread.
b: Uncomplicated cystitis: no fever, no flank pain.
Complicated cystitis: fever, flank pain, pregnancy, diabetes, catheter.
Pyelonephritis: fever, chills, flank pain, costovertebral angle tenderness.
Urosepsis: hypotension, altered mental status, organ dysfunction.

sections.p: The majority of UTIs are caused by gram‑negative rods, especially E. coli, that ascend from the perineum. Other organisms include Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus, and in low‑resource settings, Staphylococcus saprophyticus and Candida.
b: E. coli (most common)
Klebsiella
Proteus
Enterococcus
Staph saprophyticus
Candida

t.b: Detects leukocyte esterase and nitrites; positive suggests bacterial infection.
Identifies organism and antibiotic susceptibility; confirms diagnosis.
Counts white cells and bacteria; helps gauge severity.

sections.p: Patients report painful urination, increased frequency, urgency, and sometimes fever. In children, fever and poor urine stream may be the only clues.
b: Adults: dysuria, frequency, suprapubic pain, low‑grade fever.
Children: fever, irritability, poor stream, abdominal pain.
Pregnancy: fever, flank pain, risk of pyelonephritis.

sections.p: Key tests confirm infection and guide therapy. In low‑resource settings, a dipstick plus microscopy may suffice when culture is unavailable.

t.b: Answers whether leukocytes or nitrites are present; a positive result supports infection.
Answers if white cells or bacteria are seen; helps estimate bacterial load.
Answers which organism is present and its antibiotic sensitivity; essential for complicated or recurrent cases.
Answers if bacteremia is present; indicated in fever, chills, or suspected sepsis.
Answers if obstruction or stones are present; indicated in recurrent or complicated UTIs.

sections.p: Urgent care is needed if there is hypotension, altered mental status, severe flank pain, or signs of sepsis. Complications include pyelonephritis, urosepsis, renal scarring, and infertility.
b: Severe flank pain with fever – possible pyelonephritis.
Hypotension or tachycardia – possible urosepsis.
Recurrent UTIs in children – risk of renal scarring.
Pregnancy with UTI – risk of preterm labor.

sections.p: Treat the identified organism with an appropriate antibiotic, considering local resistance. Supportive care includes hydration and pain control. Monitor for treatment failure or complications.
b: First‑line: nitrofurantoin or trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole for uncomplicated cystitis.
Second‑line: fluoroquinolones or beta‑lactams for resistant strains.
Avoid: fluoroquinolones in pregnancy; avoid NSAIDs in severe infection.
Supportive: oral fluids, analgesia, and monitoring of symptoms.

sections.p: Re‑check urine after treatment if symptoms persist. Prevention focuses on hydration, proper perineal hygiene, and early treatment of asymptomatic bacteriuria in high‑risk groups.
b: Encourage 2–3 L of water daily.
Use front‑to‑back wiping.
Avoid unnecessary catheter use.
Screen pregnant women for asymptomatic bacteriuria.

sections.p: UTI can mimic prostatitis, interstitial cystitis, and sexually transmitted infections. Distinguishing features include fever and leukocytes for UTI, versus chronic pain without infection for interstitial cystitis.
b: Prostatitis – fever, chills, and pelvic pain.
Interstitial cystitis – chronic pain without infection.
Sexually transmitted infections – urethral discharge, genital lesions.

sections.p: Dipstick may be negative in early infection or with low bacterial load. Microscopy can miss bacteria in dilute samples. Culture may be delayed or unavailable in low‑resource settings.
b: False‑negative dipstick in early UTI.
Low urine volume dilutes cells and bacteria.
Delayed culture results delay targeted therapy.

whenToSeekHelp: Persistent fever after 48 hours of therapy

faq.a: Yes, especially in pregnant women or catheterised patients; screening is recommended in these groups.

faq.q: Why is nitrofurantoin used for uncomplicated cystitis?
faq.a: It concentrates in urine, has broad gram‑negative coverage, and is safe for most patients except pregnancy and renal impairment.

faq.q: When should I use a fluoroquinolone?
faq.a: When local resistance to first‑line agents is high or the infection is complicated; avoid in pregnancy and in patients with tendon disorders.

exam: Explain the diagnostic criteria for uncomplicated cystitis and why a urine culture is not always needed.
Describe the management plan for a pregnant woman with a positive urine culture for E. coli.
Identify red flags that would change a simple UTI into a case of urosepsis.
